today.subtitle: The AI Supercycle is accelerating industrial production faster than financial markets are willing to finance it — and industrial velocity and financial velocity are diverging.
today.standfirst: The ultimate scarcity of the AI Supercycle is becoming the capacity to finance sustained technological acceleration while preserving the economic returns that make acceleration possible.

nextEconomy.title: Next Economy Dashboard
nextEconomy.hypothesis: The AI supercycle is producing record revenues, but electricity delays are beginning to destroy financial value, and the market is learning to tell the difference. Capital determines what can be financed; electricity determines what can be delivered.

rows.reading: Grid delay hit contracted revenue and repriced the equity; liquidity of A$8.675B means it is not imminent distress.
Cut of roughly 22% at the midpoint after Jemena suspended upgrades for the M3 Melbourne facility.
Cut of roughly 36% at the midpoint; the next grid supply increase is not expected until fiscal 2028.
Deferred commissioning, with service-level credits and, in some cases, customer termination rights.
Hardware demand is accelerating; gross margin is expected at 12–12.5%. Final results are due November 3.
Rapid revenue from renting existing computing capacity; consolidated revenue was $14.58B, up 161%.
Expected to rise further; durable returns depend on incremental margins, depreciation, customer concentration and free cash flow.
Financial capital is moving faster than physical infrastructure; grid-connection queues in some jurisdictions exceed existing peak demand, though they include speculative and duplicated applications.
Weak industrial output despite strong AI-related earnings.
Partly driven by energy profits and data-centre suppliers; Europe may capture value via ASML, ABB, Schneider Electric and Siemens.
The market is becoming more selective rather than uniformly distressed.
Financing for developers is demanding; it points to selection, not uniform distress.
